planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Christmas is valued in South Florida and the Gulf South for ripening its orange-fleshed fruit unusually early, often just after the winter holidays.

directions: Site Christmas loquat in full sun on well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, and protect the fall bloom from hard freezes since flower and young-fruit damage below the mid-20s F is the main limit on cropping in zone 8b-9. This cultivar was selected in Florida for a markedly early ripening window, often filling the gap before the main January-March loquat harvest that most other cultivars occupy. Fruits are medium-sized with orange flesh and a bright, tangy-sweet flavor typical of Florida-bred selections rather than the milder Californian white-fleshed types. Thin heavy fruit clusters to improve size and reduce limb breakage, and pick fruit only after full color develops since loquats do not ripen further once removed from the tree.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension - Loquat Production
California Rare Fruit Growers Association - Loquat Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full to partial sun; like other white-fleshed loquats, Fletcher White benefits from a sheltered planting site since its late-winter bloom is frost-sensitive.

directions: Grow Fletcher White in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, giving it room to reach its mature rounded canopy. It belongs to the white-fleshed group of loquat cultivars, alongside Champagne and Vista White, prized for a delicate, low-acid, almost pear-like sweetness rather than the tangier orange-fleshed types. The medium to large fruits ripen in a tight cluster in late winter to early spring and are best harvested by hand as each fruit colors fully, since uneven ripening within a cluster is common. Provide supplemental irrigation during fruit swell for larger, juicier fruit, and thin crowded clusters to reduce disease pressure in humid Gulf Coast summers following harvest.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers Association - Loquat Fruit Facts
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension - Fruit and Nut Resources

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun; Herd's Mammoth needs a sturdy support structure or careful pruning since its unusually large fruit can weigh down and split young branches.

directions: This old California heirloom loquat is grown chiefly for producing some of the largest individual fruits of any named loquat cultivar, with an orange, mildly sweet flesh and a correspondingly large seed cavity. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil with generous spacing, since the vigorous growth habit and heavy fruit clusters need room to develop without crowding. Thin fruit aggressively after fruit set to concentrate size and prevent limb sag, and stake or brace young scaffold branches during the first heavy crop. As with all loquats, protect the fall-to-winter bloom period from freezes, since flower loss is the main obstacle to consistent cropping in zone 8b.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers Association - Loquat Fruit Facts
University of California Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Strawberry loquat's bright acidity makes it a favorite for fresh eating and preserves alike in Gulf Coast home orchards.

directions: Strawberry loquat takes its name from a distinctive bright, tangy-sweet flavor reminiscent of the namesake fruit, setting it apart from milder cultivars. Grow in full sun on well-drained, organically rich soil, and water regularly during fruit development to maximize juiciness and reduce fruit-splitting. The orange-fleshed fruit ripens in a compact cluster in late winter to early spring; harvest by clipping whole clusters or picking individual fruits as they fully color, since loquats do not sweeten further after picking. Prune lightly after harvest to maintain an open canopy that promotes air circulation and reduces fruit rot in humid Gulf Coast conditions.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers Association - Loquat Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Loquat Production

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun; Thales is a moderately vigorous, reliably productive orange-fleshed loquat suited to home orchard use in zone 8b-10.

directions: Thales produces large, orange-fleshed fruit with a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor and is valued as a reliable, moderately vigorous grower for home orchard plantings. Site trees in full sun on well-drained soil and provide even soil moisture through the late-winter bloom and spring fruit development period, since drought stress at fruit set can reduce yield. Thin clusters to improve individual fruit size and stake young trees carrying their first heavy crop to prevent branch breakage. As with all loquat cultivars, a sheltered microclimate away from cold pockets improves cropping consistency in the cooler end of its Gulf Coast range.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers Association - Loquat Fruit Facts
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension - Fruit and Nut Resources

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun; Victory is known for vigorous growth and dependable heavy cropping once established in zone 8b-10 gardens.

directions: Victory loquat is grown for its vigorous habit and heavy, dependable fruit set, producing orange-fleshed fruit of good size and pleasant sweet-tart flavor over a long harvest window in late winter to spring. Plant in full sun on deep, well-drained soil and allow ample spacing for its larger-than-average mature canopy. Because Victory tends to set fruit prolifically, thin clusters after fruit set to prevent overcropping, which can lead to smaller fruit and biennial bearing. Protect the fall bloom from hard freezes, and mulch well to conserve soil moisture through the humid Gulf Coast growing season.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers Association - Loquat Fruit Facts
University of California Cooperative Extension

common_name: Trask Feijoa (Historic Large-Fruited California Pineapple Guava)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun to light shade; Trask is one of the original named feijoa cultivars from early-1900s California selection trials and benefits from a cross-pollinator such as Coolidge or Apollo for heavier fruit set.

directions: Trask is one of the earliest named feijoa selections from California, dating to the early twentieth century, and remains valued for producing medium-large, oblong fruit with good aromatic flavor. Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and interplant with a second cultivar to improve pollination and yield, since Trask sets fruit more reliably with a cross-pollinator nearby. The silvery-green evergreen foliage and showy edible-petaled spring flowers make Trask a useful dual-purpose edible landscape shrub. Harvest fruit as it drops naturally in fall, and prune lightly after harvest only to shape, since fruit forms on the current season's wood.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers Association - Feijoa Fruit Facts
New Zealand Institute for Plant and Food Research - Feijoa Variety Notes

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Pendolino is a heavy pollen producer widely interplanted with Frantoio and Leccino to boost fruit set on those varieties.

directions: Pendolino is a classic Tuscan olive cultivar grown chiefly as a highly effective, long-blooming pollinizer for other Italian varieties, though its own fruit also produces good-quality oil. Plant in full sun on well-drained, low-fertility, neutral to alkaline soil, and site it within bee-flight range of Frantoio, Leccino, or Maurino to maximize cross-pollination across the planting. The tree's distinctive weeping, willowy branch habit gives it ornamental value beyond fruit production. Pendolino shows reasonable cold tolerance for an Italian olive variety, making it a workable choice for zone 8b-9 Gulf Coast plantings where a dedicated pollinizer tree improves overall grove yield.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension - Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension - Olive Production in Texas

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Maurino is prized among Italian cultivars for above-average cold tolerance, an asset for marginal zone 8b Gulf Coast sites.

directions: Maurino is an Italian oil olive noted for early, precocious bearing and comparatively strong cold hardiness within the Olea europaea cultivar group, which has made it a popular choice for growers testing olives at the cooler margins of their range. Plant in full sun in well-drained, low-fertility, neutral to alkaline soil, and expect Maurino to begin cropping earlier in tree life than many traditional Italian varieties. It is partially self-fertile but produces a heavier, more consistent crop with a cross-pollinator such as Frantoio or Pendolino nearby. Harvest fruit in late fall as color shifts from green to purple for oil production, and irrigate sparingly since Maurino, like most olives, tolerates drought well once its root system is established.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension - Olive Varieties
California Olive Committee

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Chemlali's strong heat and drought tolerance make it a good candidate for the hot, humid summers of the Gulf Coast.

directions: Chemlali is Tunisia's dominant olive variety, prized for exceptional heat and drought tolerance and dual use for both oil and cured table olives. Plant in full sun on well-drained, low-fertility soil, where it will tolerate the intense summer heat of the Gulf Coast better than many cooler-climate Mediterranean cultivars. It is only partially self-fertile, so plant a second cultivar such as Arbequina or Koroneiki nearby to ensure good fruit set. Harvest green for brine-cured table olives in early fall, or allow fruit to darken into November for oil pressing. Established Chemlali trees need very little supplemental irrigation once their deep root system is in place.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension - Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension - Olive Production in Texas

common_name: Barnea Olive (Self-Fertile Heat-Tolerant Israeli Oil Olive)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Barnea is self-fertile, heat-tolerant, and widely planted by home orchardists across the warmer parts of Texas and the Gulf South.

directions: Barnea is a modern Israeli olive cultivar bred for productivity, self-fertility, and adaptability to hot climates, which has made it a favorite among home growers experimenting with olives outside the classic Mediterranean growing zones. Plant in full sun on well-drained, low-fertility, neutral to alkaline soil; because Barnea is self-fertile it will crop reliably as a single tree, though yields improve further with a second variety nearby. It tolerates the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers better than many older European cultivars and produces good-quality oil with a robust, peppery flavor. Harvest in late fall as fruit color darkens, and prune annually to maintain an open center that improves fruit quality and reduces disease pressure in humid climates.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension - Olive Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension - Olive Production in Texas

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root plants in late winter to spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Provence is a French heirloom valued for good cold tolerance and reliable fruiting in marginal pomegranate climates.

directions: Provence is a French pomegranate selection grown for its combination of good cold hardiness and consistently sweet-tart, well-balanced fruit, making it a useful choice at the cooler edge of pomegranate country. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; established plants tolerate drought and poor soils well, though even moisture during fruit development improves size and reduces splitting. Fruit is medium-sized with a reddish-pink rind and juicy, pink-red arils that ripen in early-to-mid fall. Prune out dead or crossing wood in late winter and remove root suckers to maintain a single- or multi-trunk shrub form suited to home garden spacing.
sources: Just Fruits and Exotics Nursery - Pomegranate Variety Notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension - Pomegranate Production

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root plants in late winter to spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Sirenevyi is a cold-hardy Russian selection known for its unusual lilac-tinted skin color.

directions: Sirenevyi is a Russian-bred pomegranate cultivar named for the distinctive lilac-purple blush of its rind, which sets it apart visually from typical red-skinned pomegranates. Bred for cold hardiness, it is a good option for growers on the cooler fringe of the Gulf Coast pomegranate range who still want reliable fruiting. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and expect a compact, multi-stemmed shrub habit that responds well to light annual pruning. Fruit has a tart-sweet flavor typical of Central Asian and Russian pomegranate breeding lines; harvest in fall once the rind fully colors and a metallic ring is heard when fruit is tapped.
sources: North American Fruit Explorers - Pomegranate Cultivar Notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension - Pomegranate Production
